title: Student influencers in Australia | MANA
description: Student influencers in Australia: dated audience data from MANA's creators, what student content actually sells, and the scope to agree before filming.
h1: Student influencers in Australia: who they reach and how brands work with them
lede: Student influencers in Australia are creators who film from inside study rather than about it, and their reach runs well past the people who follow them. Two of the three creators MANA represents work in that space: Kevin Chiang drew 928K+ monthly views at 92% non-follower reach (Instagram insights, 30 days, June 2026), and Preston Young, a student at the University of Melbourne, drew 1.86M views in 90 days (Instagram insights, June to September 2026).

sections.h2: What counts as a student influencer?
body: A creator whose content is set in study: the software, the tools, the desk, the routine, the lessons that come out of it. The audience is mostly people in the same years of life, which is why the category suits software, tech, tools, food and training products more than it suits luxury.

Kevin Chiang makes architecture and design content for students, young architects and creatives, and lists student life among his audience interests. Preston Young studies at the University of Melbourne and makes story-led reels across life lessons, self-growth, day in the life, student life and fitness. Neither is a campus ambassador account. They are creators first, with study as the setting.

sections.h2: Who do student creators actually reach?
body: Not only students, and not only Australia. Kevin's audience is 56.5% aged 18 to 24 and 31.6% aged 25 to 34, so 88% sits in the 18 to 34 band, and the gender split is even at 49% male and 51% female. His biggest follower markets are India at 12.1%, Australia at 9.2% and the USA at 6.9%, with Melbourne the largest single city at 6.2%. Source: Instagram insights, 30 days, June 2026.

Preston's audience is older and male-led: 43.5% aged 25 to 34, 23.2% aged 18 to 24, 65% male. His top markets are the US at 18.0%, the Philippines at 16.1% and Indonesia at 7.2%, with Singapore the top city at 11.3%. Source: Instagram insights, 90 days, June to September 2026.

The figure to plan against is non-follower reach: 92% of Kevin's reach and 86.6% of Preston's comes from people who do not follow them. Follower counts in this bracket are small and tell you very little. Views, unique viewers and saves tell you what a placement will actually sit inside. For the design-led half of the same audience, the numbers are set out in [architecture and design influencers in Australia](/journal/architecture-and-design-influencers-australia).

Saves are the signal in this category. A student who saves a tools reel comes back to it when the assignment is due, which is why sign-ups keep arriving after the first week. A reach-only report will miss that entirely, so ask for saves and shares alongside views.

sections.h2: How do brands work with student creators?
body: The same way as with any creator, with one extra variable: the academic calendar. Assessment and exam weeks are fixed and non-negotiable, so a live date agreed without checking them is the first thing to break. Agree filming and posting dates against the semester, and leave a buffer for approvals.

The rest is scope. Deliverables, revisions, usage window, whitelisting, exclusivity and dates go in writing before anything is filmed, and the usage window is where most disputes start. If you plan to run the content as an ad, say so in the brief rather than after the post performs, and read [usage rights and whitelisting, explained for brands](/journal/usage-rights-and-whitelisting-explained-for-brands) first.

MANA handles that side for its three creators, from the first email to the live post, with one contact. If you want the roster and audience data in one place, start at the page on how to [work with Australian content creators](/brands).

A common way it goes wrong: the scope is agreed over direct messages, the product arrives late, the shoot lands in exam week, and the brand then asks to run the reel as a paid ad that was never priced or permitted. Everything in that chain is avoidable in writing.

sections.h2: Checklist: settle this before anything is filmed
body: Send this with the brief and you remove almost every later argument.
bullets: Deliverables and formats, named: reel, carousel, story frames, raw UGC.
Filming and live dates checked against assessment and exam weeks.
Revisions capped at a number, with a feedback deadline attached.
Usage rights: which channels, which window, agreed in writing rather than assumed.
Whitelisting or partnership ads named separately if you intend to run paid.
Category exclusivity, if you want it, with a length and a defined category.
Reporting you will receive: views, unique viewers, saves, shares.
Disclosure: the paid partnership label stays on.

faq: Do student influencers only reach students?

No. Both of MANA's creators in this space reach mostly 18 to 34 year olds, but Preston Young's audience is 43.5% aged 25 to 34 and male-led at 65%, with its largest markets in the US, the Philippines and Indonesia. Kevin Chiang's is 88% aged 18 to 34 and evenly split by gender, with India, Australia and the USA on top. Treat student content as a format and a setting, not a guarantee of a student-only audience.
Is a creator with a small following worth booking?

Look at reach instead of followers. In the 30 days to June 2026, Kevin Chiang's content drew 928K+ views and 359K unique viewers with 92% non-follower reach. Preston Young drew 1.86M views and 1.09M unique viewers over 90 days to September 2026 at 86.6% non-follower reach, with six reels past 750K views in 12 months. Those numbers come from the creators' own Instagram insights.
